title: Elastic strain energy; Gas laws and ideal gas equation; Temperature, internal energy, thermal equilibrium
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: MT03-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; MT03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; T05-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; MT03-1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: MT03-1#N.4, T01-1#N.2, T05-1#N.2a, MT03-1#N.8, T01-1#N.5, T05-1#N.6, MT03-1#N.11, T01-1#N.9a, T05-1#N.9a, T01-1#N.11, T05-1#N.12.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Limit of proportionality
items.clue: Point beyond which a force–extension graph curves, so only the area gives the work done.

items.label: Elastic strain energy
items.clue: Work stored in a stretched spring or wire in its Hooke's law region, returned on unloading.

items.label: Absolute zero
items.clue: The temperature 0 K, about –273 °C, where an extended pressure line for any gas meets the axis.

items.label: Internal energy
items.clue: Where most of the work goes when a sample is stretched into its plastic region: the sample warms.

questions.stem: A steel wire obeys Hooke's law. A tension of 60 N gives an extension of 1.2 mm. How much elastic strain energy does the wire store?
questions.explanation: Energy = ½ × force × extension = ½ × 60 × 1.2 × 10⁻³ = 0.036 J.

questions.stem: A 0.20 kg copper block at 80 °C is lowered into a large tank containing 200 kg of water at 20 °C. The water has far more internal energy than the block. Which statement describes the resultant thermal energy transfer?

options.text: From the block to the water, until they reach the same temperature.
From the water to the block, since the water has more internal energy.
Coldness passes from the water into the block, so the block cools down.
From the block to the water, until they have equal internal energies.

questions.stem: A cylinder contains 0.64 kg of oxygen gas, which consists of O₂ molecules. The molar mass of oxygen atoms is 16 g mol⁻¹, and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many oxygen molecules are in the cylinder?

The spring in a toy dart launcher has a spring constant of 400 N m⁻¹. It is compressed by 0.030 m and then released, firing a dart of mass 0.012 kg horizontally. All the elastic potential energy is transferred to the dart's kinetic energy. What is the speed of the dart?

options.text: 7.7 m s⁻¹
5.5 m s⁻¹
30 m s⁻¹
3.9 m s⁻¹

questions.stem: Sample P is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C. Sample Q is warmed from 290 K to 310 K. Which statement about the two temperature changes is correct?

options.text: P's rise of 20 °C is equivalent to a rise of 293 K.
The changes differ, since kelvins and °C differ in size.
Both undergo the same temperature change, 20 K.
P's rise is larger, since P's temperature tripled.

questions.stem: Predict first. Students measure the pressure of three samples of gas, each sealed in a rigid container, at several temperatures between 0 °C and 100 °C. The samples are of different gases and different amounts, and each behaves as an ideal gas. For each sample they plot pressure against temperature in °C and get a straight line. They then extend each best-fit line to zero pressure. What do they find?

options.text: All three lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature, 0 °C.
All three lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature, about −273 °C.
The steepest line reaches zero pressure at the highest temperature.
Each line reaches zero pressure at a temperature set by its kind of gas.

questions.stem: A spring obeys Hooke's law. When it is compressed by 3.0 cm it stores 0.45 J. How much energy does it store when it is compressed by 4.5 cm?
questions.explanation: Energy ∝ (compression)². The compression is 1.5 times larger, so E = 0.45 × 1.5² = 1.0 J.

questions.stem: You have 1.0 kg of ice at 0 °C and 1.0 kg of liquid water at 0 °C. Which statement about their internal energies is correct?

options.text: They are equal, since both are at the same temperature.
The water has more: its molecules have more potential energy.
The ice has more, since strong forces hold its molecules in place.
The water has more, since its molecules move faster on average.

questions.explanation: Melting takes in energy with no rise in temperature. That energy separates the molecules, raising their potential energy; their mean kinetic energy is unchanged.

questions.stem: A bubble of gas of volume 2.0 cm³ is released at the bottom of a lake, where the pressure is 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the temperature is 7 °C. It rises to the surface, where the pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the temperature is 17 °C. Treat the gas as ideal, with no gas gained or lost. What is its volume at the surface?

options.text: 6.0 cm³
15 cm³
6.2 cm³
0.69 cm³

questions.explanation: pressure × volume ÷ T is constant: V₂ = 2.0 × (3.0 × 10⁵/1.0 × 10⁵) × (290/280) = 6.2 cm³.

questions.stem: A thermometer at room temperature, 20 °C, is placed in a cup of water at 70 °C. Its reading rises for a while and then stays steady. Why does the steady reading give the temperature of the water?

options.text: All energy transfer between the thermometer and the water has then stopped completely for good.
The thermometer then has as much internal energy as the water in the cup, so the two readings match.
The cold in the thermometer has then all flowed out into the water, so it can read correctly.
They are then in thermal equilibrium, so no net energy is transferred between them.

questions.stem: A sealed, rigid container holds an ideal gas at 7 °C. The gas is heated to 287 °C. How does its new pressure compare with its starting pressure?

options.text: It is the same, because the container is rigid, so the volume cannot change.
It is 41 times as large, because the temperature has risen from 7 °C to 287 °C.
It is twice as large, because the absolute temperature doubles, from 280 K to 560 K.
It is 1.4 times as large, because the molecules move √2 times as fast.

questions.explanation: At constant volume, pressure ÷ absolute temperature is constant. 560 K/280 K = 2.
